title: China could supply EV manufacturing boom with recycled EVs
gist: A Joule study led by Xin Xiong at Nanjing University models Chinese EV material supply from 2010 to 2050 and finds recycling could become the dominant source of many key battery and motor materials — but element by element, with cobalt going into recycled surplus as chemistries shift away from it while nickel and manganese demand outruns recycled supply. The economics hinge on a perverse feedback: cheaper chemistries like sodium make batteries less valuable to recyclers, the same reason graphite is largely not recycled today.

themes.theme: The circularity model and its scope

insights.claim: A study led by Xin Xiong at Nanjing University finds that in China, recycling could become the dominant source of many key materials needed to manufacture EV components over the coming decades.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: If domestic scrap becomes the marginal supply source, China's long-run import dependence on battery and rare-earth feedstock falls — a structural bear case for virgin-material producers selling into China.
insights.locator: Still, a study led by Xin Xiong at Nanjing University

insights.claim: The model spans 2010 to 2050 and covers battery materials across hybrid, battery-electric and fuel-cell vehicles — lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, phosphorus, sodium, sulfur and graphite — plus critical motor elements copper, neodymium, dysprosium, samarium and cerium.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Element-level coverage is what makes this usable for commodity work — the aggregate 'recycling wins' headline hides opposite conclusions per metal.

insights.claim: The study's central metric is 'circularity potential' — how much of a given year's manufacturing demand for an element can be supplied by the flow of recycled material in that same year.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Same-year flow matching is the right lens for supply planning because stock-based recycling rates overstate near-term availability.
insights.locator: The model calculates the “circularity potential” of each element

insights.claim: The researchers ran four technological-progression scenarios — slow transition to solid-state lithium, sodium batteries and reduced-rare-earth motors, faster transition, complete transition to new chemistries, and a decade-by-decade progression through the first three — each modeled at both 40 percent and 100 percent vehicle recycling rates.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: The scenario spread is the uncertainty band to quote when someone claims a single number for future recycled supply.
insights.locator: The researchers considered four scenarios for technological progression

insights.claim: Cobalt flips into structural surplus: as the industry pivots to low-cobalt battery chemistries, demand falls while recycled supply from scrapped EVs keeps rising, so recycled cobalt quickly exceeds demand.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Falling demand plus rising secondary supply is a double hit to cobalt pricing — the clearest directional commodity call in the study.

insights.claim: Nickel and manganese demand for batteries could increase drastically over time, keeping the share that recycling can supply relatively flat despite growing scrap volumes.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Nickel and manganese stay mining-dependent even under aggressive recycling — the opposite trade to cobalt.
insights.locator: Conversely, the amount of nickel and manganese needed

insights.claim: Motor-element circularity is highly sensitive to which technology wins — for instance whether cerium is used to displace more expensive rare-earth elements — so rare-earth supply conclusions are scenario-contingent rather than robust.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Rare-earth demand forecasts should be treated as options on motor design choices, not as extrapolations of EV unit growth.
insights.locator: The story for elements in motors is similar

insights.claim: Battery-electric vehicle sales keep rising all the way to 2050 in the model while hybrids and plug-in hybrids fade out, so the flow of vehicles reaching recyclers steadily increases but structurally lags new manufacturing demand.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: A growing fleet mechanically caps circularity — recycling cannot close the gap while unit sales compound, which is why mining demand persists through the transition.
insights.locator: Though hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles eventually fade out

insights.claim: Chinese policy targets raising recycling rates for certain battery elements from the current 40 percent to a standard of at least 98 percent, and raising the EV share of new sales from 45 percent to 60 percent by 2030.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: A 40-to-98 percent mandated jump is the single biggest swing factor in the model's outputs — track actual compliance rates as the leading indicator for secondary supply.
insights.locator: It also factors in recent Chinese policies

insights.claim: China is mandating 'battery passports' that identify each battery and its chemical makeup and is pushing to force more scrapped batteries to officially licensed recyclers, addressing the traceability and leakage problems that undermine recovery rates.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Battery passports are the enabling infrastructure for high-yield recycling — jurisdictions without them will underperform their stated targets.
insights.locator: China is using regulations to address a couple of issues

insights.claim: China has not yet mandated any level of recycled content in new battery production, leaving demand-side pull for secondary material unlegislated even as collection is being tightened.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: A recycled-content mandate is the obvious next policy shoe to drop and would immediately reprice secondary material against virgin feedstock.
insights.locator: But the researchers also note that China has yet to mandate

insights.claim: The researchers warn the complex recycling chain will be vulnerable to bottlenecks as it rapidly scales up to handle more electric vehicles over time, so headline circularity numbers depend on chain execution rather than theoretical recovery limits.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Capacity and logistics in the collection-to-refining chain, not chemistry, are where the recycling thesis most plausibly fails.
insights.locator: And they say the complex recycling chain will be vulnerable

themes.theme: The economics that decide whether it happens

insights.claim: Recycling's binding constraint is economic rather than physical: recovered materials frequently cannot compete with virgin materials on cost, which is why the mathematically obvious response to finite resources often fails commercially.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Any recycling forecast that does not model the virgin-material cost curve is a materials-flow exercise, not an investable one.
insights.quote: While recycling is a mathematically obvious response to the finite, non-renewable nature of many resources, the economic math is often challenging.
insights.locator: While recycling is a mathematically obvious response

insights.claim: Fast-moving battery technology structurally devalues recycling because by the time a car is scrapped the industry may have moved to a different battery chemistry, reducing the value of putting that battery's materials back into the production chain.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Technology churn is a hidden discount rate on recycling assets — faster innovation cycles reduce the terminal value of today's recycling capacity.
insights.locator: Fast-moving technologies like electric vehicles throw in an added complication

insights.claim: Cheaper chemistries are a double-edged sword for circularity: sodium batteries lower battery cost but make the contents less valuable to recyclers — the same economics that leave graphite in batteries largely unrecycled today.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Cost-down chemistry roadmaps and circularity goals are in direct tension — expect recycled-content mandates or subsidies to be required wherever scrap value falls.
insights.locator: Just as the graphite in batteries is often not recycled now

insights.claim: The model assumes battery replacement will be common because batteries lose capacity long before a vehicle reaches end-of-life, especially in heavy-use commercial settings, and China's battery-swapping stations add further batteries manufactured and recycled outside the vehicle-scrappage cycle.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Battery flows decouple from vehicle flows, so battery-swap infrastructure is quietly an accelerant for recycled supply years ahead of fleet scrappage.
insights.locator: The model assumes that battery replacement will be common
